# Chlorine, bleaching powder and disinfection (`chlorine_bleach`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by hydrochloric_acid_aqua_regia, lime_burning, electrolysis, alkali_soda
- Core idea: Hydrochloric acid warmed with black manganese ore (pyrolusite) gives a heavy yellow-green gas, chlorine. Passed over trays of slaked lime it is absorbed to a dry bleaching powder that can be stored and shipped; passed into cold potash or soda lye it gives a bleaching liquor. These whiten linen, cotton and paper pulp in hours instead of months on the grass, remove the smell of decay, and kill disease agents on hands, in wards and in water. For drinking water, effectiveness depends on clarity, pH, contact time and the free chlorine remaining afterwards; smell cannot establish a safe residual.
- Pitfalls:
  - Chlorine gas is a lung poison and was a weapon in 1915; an open window or outdoor work does not reliably protect workers or bystanders.
  - Mixing bleach with acids (or vinegar) releases chlorine; with ammonia or urine it gives other poisonous gases.
  - Bleach left too long or too strong rots cloth; rinse treated fibres thoroughly. Adding acid to residual bleach releases toxic gas.
  - Bleaching powder loses strength in damp and warmth; wool and silk are destroyed by it.
  - Overdosing drinking water, or thinking it clears muddy water; filter or settle first.
- History: europe: 1774 – Scheele isolates the gas; 1785 Berthollet bleaches with it; 1789 eau de Javel; 1799 Tennant's bleaching powder (Glasgow); 1820s Labarraque disinfects with it; 1847 Semmelweis uses chlorinated lime for hand washing; 1810 Davy shows it is an element; global: 1897 Maidstone and 1908 Jersey City – first chlorination of public water supplies; 1890s chlorine by electrolysis of brine
- Read:
  - Archibald Clow & Nan L. Clow, The Chemical Revolution (1952)
  - L. F. Haber, The Chemical Industry during the Nineteenth Century (1958)
